claims.statement: Life satisfaction rises with income only up to about $75,000 a year (or perhaps as high as $120,000), and no further.
Above about $75,000 a year (or perhaps $120,000), more income no longer goes with better day-to-day emotions.
Getting more money once basic needs are met (a lottery prize, a cash gift, a raise) does not make people lastingly happier or more satisfied.

notFound: no meta-analysis or multi-lab replication of an individual plateau (life satisfaction or emotions): plateaus come from cross-sectional models (Jebb, Bennedsen) or country averages (Röck, Proto, Easterlin)
no independent replication on new data of Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers 2023: only two letters on the same data (Arslan, Rohrer & Wenz)
no published version of Tamberg 2024 (preprint), Miller 2024 (NBER) or Jaroszewicz 2022 (SSRN)
no Egyptian or Arab sample in a lottery, a cash transfer or a trial; no Egyptian study with measured income that tests a threshold
no estimate for Egypt alone in Jebb 2018: its 20,924 Egyptian respondents are pooled in the MENA region
Manson's chapter 4 not read (no copy of the book): only his 2018 article and its note 4 are checked

found.note: meta-analysis, 86 studies: leaving poverty d = 0.38 (wellbeing) and 0.13 (mental health) vs 0.16 and 0.01 for other rises; GRADE low or very low: c3 mixed, c4 supported; on screen
independent reanalysis of the same data: no clear flattening before $200,000; the « least happy » plateau is weak: that nuance is withdrawn
a percentile is not a group of people: nothing on screen may say « for the least happy people »; no covariates, so no causal reading

Killingsworth, Kahneman & Mellers 2024 reply (refused by the verifier as a letter): K&D's $75,000 was the midpoint of a $60-90K band; threshold $100,000 after inflation; all quantiles but the 15th rise
2.05 million US adults: above ~$63,000, stress more likely: supports c2, so c2 cannot be « contradicts » under the grid
emotional plateau near $200,000, hedged by its author: a plateau may exist, far above $75,000-120,000
random postcode lottery (about 8 months of income): not happier six months later: supports c3
three panels (US, South Korea): changes in income unrelated to changes in well-being: supports c3
17 RCTs, poor households: depression lower while cash is paid, not sustained 2-9 years after: supports « not lastingly », indirect
German winners: no mental-health gain (high education), a loss (low education), yet they report being happier; at odds with Gardner 2006
income predicts life evaluation, much less feelings; basic needs mediate only partly: the nuance said, and against the « needs » explanation
the ladder question primes wealth: a risk of bias for the life-evaluation evidence of c1
Egypt: average happiness 4.8/10; Egyptians judge their lives poorly but feel fairly well day to day: the nuance holds for Egypt
Tamberg et al. 2024, preprint (Research Square), no published version: once needs are met, income adds marginally to life evaluation; refused by the verifier; it controls for the needs income buys
Tan et al. 2020, meta-analysis of 357 studies: the income link is stronger in wealthier samples, against Howell 2008; refused by the verifier (false positive on « the objective »)
Proto & Rustichini 2013: country-level satisfaction flattens above ~$15,000 GDP per head, peaks near $30,000: aggregate, indirect for c1
Easterlin et al. 2010: no long-term link between national growth and happiness, also in developing countries: aggregate, indirect
Fors Connolly et al. 2026: across 33 European countries GDP goes with both emotions and satisfaction: against Röck 2025
Quispe-Torreblanca et al. 2026, 109 countries: well-being follows income rank more than income, more so in materialistic countries
Apouey & Clark 2015: the same British panel as Gardner 2006, positive mental-health effect: not independent evidence
Kim & Oswald 2021, Singapore: corrected for ticket spending, a windfall predicts more happiness: against c3 (cross-sectional)
Miller et al. 2024 (NBER, RCT, $1,000 a month for 3 years): short-lived gains in stress, no mental-health gain after year 1
a correction to Oishi 2022 not linked in Crossref: the verifier's corrections check reads only updated-by

counterEvidence.conclusion: ⚖️ holds, low; ❌ is not defensible.
